en: Biography of Fu-jun Cunhui. Fu-jun’s name was Cunhui;
his courtesy name was Chayuan; his sobriquet was Huaiqi-yi. From youth, he harbored a gentle disposition and embraced the Way of both civil and military arts.
He combined the sincerity of both leniency and severity to jointly accomplish virtuous deeds, whether on horseback or at the bow. His archery was masterful.
However, the monkey had previously been well-versed in the deployment of battle arrays; thus,
he leaped about with unrestrained freedom and was able to join his peers,
moving with such agility that he surpassed the ordinary herd.
In all his residences and undertakings,
he alone stood out among the many eminent scholars;
all were in harmony, and the multitude raised him up together.
When recommending others, he frequently sought those who had undergone ritual purification;

when the sovereign was cautious in his seeking, he would then recommend them for promotion to official ranks, yet he did not record these appointments. He maintained a pure and reverent demeanor, fearing that others might discover his actions.
May Bao Yue surpass the worthies of former generations;
may contentment exceed that of later disciples.
Thus shall it be within the gates of the military camp.
While serving as a minister to the sovereign with schemes and stratagems to assist the state amidst the anxieties of the provinces and prefectures,
who would have expected that the earth-fire would secretly turn its back?
The spirit returns to the eternal void;
the skin and flesh of the White King remain,
yet we no longer hear his beautiful words of gold.
The wife remains in her widow’s chamber, where blood and tears mingle;
such a person is as rare in this world as fish gills,
and after our parting, we must rely upon the "bird-letter" (a letter written in a cursive script resembling bird tracks).
He then requested a red brush to record the features of his countenance and invited Confucian scholars to compose praises for his refined excellence.
He then praised him, saying:
"The Prefect’s natural appearance and his divine principles are manifold."
Upon entering the multitude, all paid him respect;
upon leaving, others found it difficult to equal him.
He requested to study under the Master Kong.
Wu bows at the altar of the King of Chu;
the honor and bounty of Your Majesty’s grace are profound.
His meritorious service is indeed manifold.
The five musical notes are complete upon the plucked strings;
the four tones are fully realized in the chanting of poetry.
He exercises comprehensive oversight over the provinces and prefectures.
The divine plan was manifest at the border;
how could one have expected the passing waters so soon?
A ghost arrived first from the hidden realm.
In the hall above, there was the sound of footsteps;
at the front of the courtyard, he vanished from sight.
The officials and attendants all moved to weep.
The wife again grieves for what was before;
she recalls the features of his life as they were,
while the noble retinue looks on at those who have come after.
In years to come, beneath the Realm of Reeds;
the waters shall forever flow toward the Yellow Springs.
To form the characters of birds, one must rely on distance.
The insect-script text further required transmission.
The Prefect’s taboo name was Cunhui,
and his courtesy name was Chayuan.
His ancestral clan was of the lineage of King Wuding of the Yin dynasty,
a descendant of Boyang of Longxi.
The genealogical records are quite clear and have been summarized here;
yet, they point to the planting of trees to designate a clan and the shooting of arrows to preserve its fragrance.
When the White Horse came from the East...
The Blue Ox went westward,
where he converted the land of Hu and left behind his descendants;
to this very day, they are the people of Dunhuang.
His great-great-grandfather was Military Commissioner Molil,
Governor of Guazhou,
and Grand Master of Purple Radiance.
Inspector-General of the Department of State Affairs, Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs,
concurrently serving as Chief Censor. Superior.
The Zhuge (Commander-in-Chief) was styled Huangzu;
he served as the Regional Commander for Administrative Affairs and held the rank of Silver Light Grand Master of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
Inspector-General;
Minister of War;
Attendant-in-Ordinary.
Serving concurrently as Grand Minister of the Censorate, with the rank of Zhuguo; his taboo name was Shaoqiu.
His imperial father was of the Guiyi Army.
Acting Regional Commander and Garrison Commander of Shicheng Town;
Silver Light Grand Master of the Court of Imperial Entertainments.
Inspector. Left Attendant-at-Horse.
Superior Horseman.
The Commandant,
whose taboo name is An, [is the father of] my deceased son,
the Inner Relative and Attendant Commandant of the Right and Left Frost.
General-in-Chief of the Cavalry and Infantry,
Trained Officer,
Acting Minister of War.
To the Imperial Mother, Lady Yin Zhuzhuyan,
concurrently Minister of State Affairs and Pillar of State,
of the Yin clan of Wuwei Commandery; [in memory of] my deceased uncle.
Record of the Regional Commander’s Enforcement and Urging Officer.
Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (Guanglu Daifu),
Acting Official.
The State Sacrificial Libationer and concurrently the Imperial Secretariat Assistant,
whose taboo name was Anding, my deceased son.
The head of the inner attendants,
Silver Light Grand Master,
Acting Official.
The aforementioned Right Attendant-at-Large and Concurrent Grand Minister of the Censorate,
Yin Zhuzhian, elder brother of the Monastic Rectifier of the Buddhist Community.
The Venerable Sramana Fading, a recipient of the purple robe,
who served as an attendant at the ritual altar and was a master of doctrinal studies; his lordship had early prepared himself with martial prowess.
His literary achievements were manifest from an early age;
yet, having only just begun to apply the principles of governing a state,
he did not succeed in fulfilling his path of assisting his sovereign.
Who would have expected that while singing together in Qi, one would secretly chant the verses of Lu?
First, the *po* rhyme was intoned, startling the waves; then the soul followed the passing waters.
On the twenty-sixth day, the *gengzi* day, of the first month of the fifth year of Taiping Xingguo, the *gengchen* year.
He lay ill upon his pillow and passed away at his private residence in Xiwen Ward.
On the third day, the third of the second month of that year, which was the day of Jiachen followed by Bingwu,
he was temporarily interred with offerings at Yang in Gaoli.
This is the rite for opening the original site at Hebei.

A separate divination has determined that the burial shall take place in the ancestral cemetery. [The names of] the sister’s son-in-law, Commander Deng Qingshun, and her nephew, Commander Cao Youchong, [are inscribed here].
Together they honor the bond of flesh and blood as kinsmen of the same branch;
some have already passed away into the realm of the dead,
while others remain present among those within and without.
Leaning against the railing, my pain was so piercing that it tore at the entrails of my younger siblings;
with my spirit exhausted and my soul dissolved, the tears of both women and men flowed together.
Thus, the affairs of the world and the passage of years shifted in private.
Fame and reputation vanish with the passing of the sun and moon;
the loss of nobility is recorded by means of bird-track inscriptions upon steles shaped like dragon heads.
The inscription reads:
"When Heaven arrays the stars and constellations, those destined for greatness must respond;
when the wind and clouds gather, the worthy and talented find their auspicious union."
The sovereign and his ministers were in rare accord, yet they did not enter [the fray].
Their conduct was as clear as ice and pure as jade;
their resolve was firm and unyielding, like a sharp blade that cannot be turned back.
I thought the village lanes would be woven together by the waters;
who would have expected that the wind would carry the soul away to the night palace?
The pines and peppers stand silent, where only foxes and hares are seen.
In the deep darkness of the grave, stone serves as the memorial;
through the distant span of a thousand autumns, what is not inscribed in the "bird-character" script?
To leave a fragrance for ten thousand years—this is surely the work of brush and ink.
Composed on the third day of the second month in the fifth year of Taiping Xingguo, the Gengchen year.
